rubric.text: Numerator reduces to $\big(\tfrac12-\tfrac1{24}\big)x^4+O(x^6)$, the $x^2$ terms cancelling with $\tfrac32x^2$

solution:
$e^{x^2}=1+x^2+\tfrac{x^4}{2}+O(x^6)$ and $\cos x=1-\tfrac{x^2}{2}+\tfrac{x^4}{24}+O(x^6)$ (taylor).
Difference: $\tfrac32x^2+\big(\tfrac12-\tfrac1{24}\big)x^4+O(x^6)$.
Subtract $\tfrac32x^2$ and divide by $x^4$ (limit-special): limit $\tfrac{11}{24}$.
L-Hopital would need four rounds of differentiation (lhopital); series is faster.
hints: Expand both functions to order $x^4$.

rubric.text: $e^{-x^2}=1-x^2+\tfrac{x^4}{2}-\tfrac{x^6}{6}+\cdots$ by substituting $-x^2$ into the exponential series

solution:
$e^{u}=\sum u^k/k!$ with $u=-x^2$ gives $e^{-x^2}=1-x^2+\tfrac{x^4}{2}-\cdots$ (taylor, exp-rules).
So $f(x)=x^2-x^4+\tfrac{x^6}{2}-\cdots$ (power-series).
The coefficient of $x^6$ is $\tfrac{f^{(6)}(0)}{6!}=\tfrac12$.
$f^{(6)}(0)=720\cdot\tfrac12=360$.
hints: Read the derivative off the coefficient of $x^6$.

rubric.text: Area $=\tfrac\pi3+4\int_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2}\cos^2\theta\,d\theta$ set up using $\tfrac12\int r^2$ and symmetry
Half-angle evaluation gives $\tfrac\pi3-\tfrac{\sqrt3}2$ for the second part; total $\tfrac{2\pi}3-\tfrac{\sqrt3}2$

solution:
Intersection: $2\cos\theta=1$ gives $\theta=\pm\tfrac\pi3$ (trig-eq). For $|\theta|<\tfrac\pi3$ the circle $r=1$ is closer to the origin; beyond that $r=2\cos\theta$ is (param-polar).
By symmetry, $A=2\Big[\tfrac12\!\int_0^{\pi/3}1\,d\theta+\tfrac12\!\int_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2}4\cos^2\theta\,d\theta\Big]=\tfrac\pi3+2\!\int_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2}(1+\cos2\theta)\,d\theta$ (trig-int).
$\big[2\theta+\sin2\theta\big]_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2}=\pi-\big(\tfrac{2\pi}3+\tfrac{\sqrt3}2\big)=\tfrac\pi3-\tfrac{\sqrt3}2$.
$A=\tfrac\pi3+\tfrac\pi3-\tfrac{\sqrt3}2=\tfrac{2\pi}3-\tfrac{\sqrt3}2$.
hints: Sketch both circles; the boundary switches curves at the intersection angle.

prompt: Find the length of the curve $x=t^2$, $y=t^3$ for $0\le t\le2$.

why: forgot the lower-limit value $-8$
dropped the factor $\tfrac23$ when integrating $\sqrt u$
used $|x^{\prime}|+|y^{\prime}|$ as the speed
computed $40^{3/2}$ as $40\sqrt{10}$

solution:
$x^{\prime}=2t$, $y^{\prime}=3t^2$, speed $=\sqrt{4t^2+9t^4}=t\sqrt{4+9t^2}$ (param-polar, arc-avg).
Let $u=4+9t^2$, $du=18t\,dt$, limits $4\to40$ (u-sub): $L=\tfrac1{18}\int_4^{40}\sqrt u\,du$.
$=\tfrac1{18}\cdot\tfrac23\big[u^{3/2}\big]_4^{40}=\tfrac1{27}\big(40^{3/2}-8\big)$.
$40^{3/2}=40\cdot2\sqrt{10}=80\sqrt{10}$, so $L=\tfrac{80\sqrt{10}-8}{27}$.
hints: Factor $t$ out of the speed so it can serve as $du$.
